newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine alumina plant still ready to sell to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine alumina plant still ready to sell to Russia.

text.p: Ukraine's largest alumina plant said on Thursday that Russian aluminium producers seemed to be using strongarm tactics to make it drop its metal prices, but it was still ready to do business with its northern neighbour.
"There are no direct discussions..." said Valery Agafonov, financial director of Mykolayivsky Hlynozemny Zavod (MHZ) in the southern city of Mykolayiv.
Agafonov said by telephone that his team heard about what seemed to be the Russian position through media reports.
"All of these comments are being made with the goal of influencing our actions and forcing us to sell our product at a lower price," Agafonov said.

The Siberian Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk smelters said on Thursday they had broken off talks with MHZ because it was demanding prices that were too high, so they would seek the metal outside the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

MHZ, which produces virtually all Ukraine's alumina, has traditionally supplied 90 percent of its output -- forecast at one million tonnes this year, the same as last -- to Russia. It produced 996,000 tonnes in 1995.
The government is expected to approve privatisation of the plant, on a list of more than 200 firms which Ukraine wants to privatise through strategic foreign investment, on February 18.

Russia depends on imports for most of its alumina and has been seeking raw materials at low prices through supply contracts with Mykolayiv, which the Ukraine plans to privatise through strategic foreign investment.
"We are prepared to continue to work with Russian aluminium smelters in 1997, especially since our plant produces 20 percent of the alumina that Russia needs," Agafonov said.
Agafonov denied that MHZ was charging above world prices. These were rising and had reached $180-190 per tonne for Australian alumina.
"But Russian aluminium plants want to buy it for $170 a tonne at Ukraine's border. This does not suit us, also because our production costs are higher than Australia's, for obvious reasons," he said.
Bauxite used to produce Ukraine's alumina is imported from West Africa. But the Bratsk plant said Mykolayiv's prices were inflated by high production costs and an overall lack of competitiveness.
Prices have firmed to around $185/190 a tonne fob Australia from $140/145 in the third quarter last year, Macquarie Equities said in a recent report.

Agafonov said the plant planned to maintain regular production levels this year since it had not lost hope it would have a market for its alumina. January and February production equalled levels of last year, he added.
The manager of the Bratsk plant said talks might re-open in March.
Part of Mykolayiv's output also goes to Ukraine's AT Zaporizhsky Aluminyovy Zavod smelter and plant officials have said they planned to sell to Tajikistan this year.
